prompt: A container packages an application together with everything it needs to run — its code, runtime, and dependencies — as one unit you can move and run anywhere.
What does a container package together?
A container packages an app together with its dependencies.
explanation: That's the whole idea — code and dependencies travel together as one unit.

prompt: A container bundles an app with its ___.
What travels with the app inside a container?

A container is isolated from the host machine — its own filesystem and processes — but it shares the host's OS kernel instead of running one of its own, which is what makes it far lighter than a full virtual machine.
What does a container share with the host?
explanation: That's also why containers avoid the heavy overhead of a full guest OS the way a VM has — they start faster and use fewer resources.

prompt: A container runs its own full operating system kernel.
explanation: It shares the host's kernel instead — that's part of what keeps it lightweight.

prompt: A container is ___ from the host machine.
What does a container avoid vs a VM?
Containers bundle the exact runtime and dependencies an app needs, so it runs the same way on your machine, a teammate's, and a server.
What problem does bundling dependencies solve?
A containerized app runs the same way everywhere.
Containers bundle the exact runtime and ___.
What did bundling dependencies fix?
Installing Docker gives you the Docker daemon that runs containers plus the docker command line tool you use to control it.
What runs your containers behind the scenes?
explanation: You control it with the docker command-line tool (the CLI), which talks to the daemon to run your commands.

prompt: The docker command talks to the Docker daemon.
The Docker ___ actually runs your containers.
What do you use to control Docker?
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of that image, the same way a class relates to an object.
What is a container relative to an image?
explanation: Because an image is read-only, running it creates a container without ever changing the original image.

prompt: An image is read-only.
An image is a ___ template for containers.
In the class analogy, an image is a ___.
docker run starts a brand-new container from an image, using that image as its starting point.
Complete: start a container from nginx.
docker ___ starts a new container.
What does docker run create?
docker run starts a container from an existing image.
explanation: That's the whole point of the command — turn an image into a running container.

prompt: If the image named in docker run isn't already on your machine, Docker automatically pulls it from a registry first, then starts the container — no separate pull step required.
docker run automatically ___ a missing image.
explanation: You never have to run docker pull first — docker run does it for you if needed.

prompt: If the image isn't local, docker run ___ it.
What happens if you docker run an unpulled image?
You must always run docker pull before docker run.
explanation: docker run pulls automatically if the image is missing.

prompt: A running container can be stopped with docker stop, which pauses it without deleting anything — the container still exists, just no longer running, until you remove it.
What stops a running container?
docker stop leaves the container still on disk, not deleted.
explanation: Stopping and removing are two separate steps.

prompt: docker ___ stops a running container.
After docker stop, is the container still there?
docker rm permanently deletes a stopped container, freeing up its name; add -f to force-remove one that's still running instead of stopping it first.
Complete: delete a stopped container.
docker rm removes a container.
docker ___ deletes a stopped container.
What does docker rm -f do?
A container moves through a predictable lifecycle: created, then running, then stopped, and finally removed.
What comes right after 'created'?
The last lifecycle stage is ___.
A container can be running before it's ever created.
explanation: Created always comes first.

prompt: Which stage comes right before 'removed'?
Docker Hub is a public registry of ready-made images, and docker pull downloads one to your machine before you ever run it.
Complete: download the redis image.
explanation: Docker Hub is the public registry these ready-made images, like redis, come from by default.

prompt: Docker Hub hosts ready-made images.
docker ___ downloads an image locally.
What is Docker Hub?
An image is built from stacked layers, and Docker caches unchanged layers so a rebuild only redoes the layers that actually changed.
What does Docker cache during a build?
explanation: Skipping unchanged layers is what makes a rebuild so much faster than starting from scratch.

prompt: An image is made of stacked layers.
Docker skips rebuilding ___ layers.
Why does layer caching help builds?
A Dockerfile is a plain text recipe of instructions that tells Docker exactly how to build your image, step by step.
What is a Dockerfile?
A Dockerfile is plain text.
A Dockerfile lists build ___ step by step.
What does a Dockerfile describe?
Every Dockerfile starts with FROM, which sets the base image your new image is built on top of.
What does FROM set?
Every Dockerfile needs a FROM instruction.
explanation: It sets the starting point everything else builds on.

prompt: ___ sets the base image a Dockerfile builds on.
What does FROM appear as in a Dockerfile?
COPY takes files from your project folder and adds them into the image being built, so your code actually ends up inside it.
What does COPY add to the image?
COPY adds files from your project into the image.
___ copies your files into the image.
Where do COPY's source files come from?
RUN executes a command during the build itself — like installing a package — and its result gets baked into the image.
What does RUN do during a build?
RUN executes while the image is being built.
___ runs a command during the build.
What commonly runs via RUN?
CMD sets the command that runs automatically when a container starts from this image — not during the build, but every time it's launched.
___ sets what runs when the container starts.
___ sets the startup command for a container.
When does CMD's command actually run?
CMD runs during the image build, not at startup.
explanation: That's what RUN is for — CMD only fires when the container starts.

prompt: docker build reads a Dockerfile and turns it into a real image you can run, tagging it with a name so you can find it later.
Complete: build and tag an image.
explanation: The -t flag names (tags) the image, e.g. myapp, so you can find and run it later.

prompt: docker build reads instructions from a Dockerfile.
docker ___ turns a Dockerfile into an image.
What does the -t flag do in docker build?
A multi-stage build uses one stage to compile your app and a leaner final stage that only copies the finished result, keeping the final image small.
What does a multi-stage build reduce?
explanation: It works by using an earlier stage to compile everything, then copying only the finished result into a leaner final stage.

prompt: A multi-stage build can use two different stages.
The final stage only copies the ___ result.
Why leave build tools out of the final stage?
A tag like myapp:1.2 names a specific version of an image, so you can pin exactly which build gets deployed.
What does an image tag identify?
A tag like myapp:1.2 identifies a specific version.
A tag lets you ___ a specific version.
What can a version tag help you do?
latest is just a regular tag name, not a magic pointer to your newest build — it only updates when you rebuild and push an image tagged latest yourself.
The latest tag is just an ordinary ___.
explanation: latest is just an ordinary tag; it only moves when you rebuild and push it.

prompt: latest is just a regular ___ name.
When does the latest tag update?
Relying on latest in prod guarantees the newest code.
A container's ports are isolated by default, so -p maps a port on your host machine to a port inside the container to reach it.
Complete: map host port 8080 to 80.
explanation: Container ports are closed off by default; -p (or its long form --publish) opens a specific mapping between a host port and a container port.

prompt: Container ports are reachable by default.
explanation: They are isolated until you explicitly map a port with -p.

prompt: The ___ flag maps a host port.
What does port mapping connect?
The -e flag passes an environment variable into a container at run time, letting the same image behave differently without rebuilding it.
Complete: set an env variable at run time.
explanation: This lets the same image behave differently in different environments without ever rebuilding it.

prompt: Env vars let one image behave differently.
The ___ flag sets an env variable.
When is an env var passed in?
A bind mount links a specific folder on your host machine straight into a container, so changes on either side show up on both, and the data survives a restart.
What does a bind mount link to a container?
A bind mount's data survives a container restart.
A bind mount links a host ___ directly.
Where does a bind mount's data actually live?
A volume is storage that Docker creates and manages for you — not a specific host folder you pick — and like a bind mount, its data survives after the container is removed.
Who manages a volume's storage?
A volume's data is lost when its container is removed.
explanation: That's the whole point of a volume — it outlives the container.

prompt: Docker ___ where a volume's data actually lives.
How does a volume differ from a bind mount?
Docker gives containers their own network by default, and containers on the same custom network can reach each other by container name.
How can containers on one network reach each other?
explanation: Every container gets its own network by default; a shared custom network is what lets them reach each other by name.

prompt: Containers get their own network by default.
Containers on a shared ___ can reach each other.
What identifies a container on a network?
docker exec -it opens an interactive shell inside a container that is already running, useful for poking around without stopping it.
Complete: open a shell in mycontainer.
explanation: This only works on a container that's already running — exec attaches to it instead of starting a new one.

prompt: docker exec works on an already-running container.
docker ___ opens a shell in a container.
Why use exec instead of stopping the container?
docker logs shows a container's console output — the same thing you'd see printed if it were running right in your terminal.
Complete: view a container's logs.
docker logs shows a container's console output.
docker ___ shows a container's output.
When might you check docker logs?
docker inspect dumps a container's full configuration — network settings, mounts, environment variables, and more — as JSON, useful when logs alone aren't enough.
Complete: view a container's full config.
docker inspect output is JSON.
docker ___ returns a container's full configuration.
What format does docker inspect use?
Flags like --memory and --cpus cap how much RAM and CPU a single container can use, so one runaway container cannot starve the whole machine.
What does --memory limit?
explanation: A matching --cpus flag caps how much CPU the container can use, the same way --memory caps RAM.

prompt: A resource limit can stop one container starving the host.
The ___ flag caps CPU usage.
Why set resource limits on a container?
A restart policy like --restart unless-stopped tells Docker to automatically bring a container back up if it crashes or the host reboots.
What does a restart policy control?
explanation: You set this with the --restart flag, e.g. --restart unless-stopped.

prompt: A restart policy can bring back a crashed container.
The ___ flag sets a restart policy.
When might a restart policy trigger?
Compose lets you define a whole set of related containers, like an app and its database, in one file, and start them together with one command.
What does Compose let you define together?
explanation: For example, an app and its database can be defined and started together instead of running separate docker run commands.

prompt: Compose can start several containers with one command.
Compose defines related services in one ___.
What can Compose group in one file?
A docker-compose.yml is a YAML file listing each service under a services key, along with its image or build path, ports, and any environment variables it needs.
In docker-compose.yml what top-level key lists your containers?
explanation: docker-compose.yml is written in YAML; each entry under services can set its own image (or build path), ports, and env vars.

prompt: A service can specify ports and env vars.
docker-compose.yml is written in ___ format.
In docker-compose.yml what can a service build from?
Compose puts all services on one shared network automatically, so a web service can reach a database service just by using its service name.
How does one Compose service reach another?
explanation: This works because Compose automatically puts every service on one shared network.

prompt: Compose puts services on a shared network automatically.
A web service reaches db by its ___ name.
What does Compose set up between services automatically?
Compose can declare named volumes for persistent data and pass in environment variables per service, keeping storage and config right next to each service.
What can a named volume give a service?
explanation: Compose services can each set their own env vars too, keeping config right alongside the service that needs it.

prompt: Each service can set its own env vars in Compose.
A named ___ keeps data across restarts.
Where does env config live in Compose?
Choosing a slim base image, combining RUN commands into fewer layers, and using multi-stage builds all keep an image small, which means faster pulls and a smaller attack surface.
Pick ways to keep an image small.
explanation: All three make pulls faster and shrink the image's attack surface.

prompt: A smaller image pulls faster.
A slim base image keeps the attack ___ small.
What can combining RUN commands reduce?
A .dockerignore file lists files and folders to exclude from the build context, like node_modules, keeping builds fast and images clean.
What does .dockerignore exclude?
explanation: A common entry is node_modules, since it's large and gets reinstalled inside the image anyway.

prompt: node_modules is a common .dockerignore entry.
.dockerignore keeps the build ___ fast.
What effect does .dockerignore have?
Baking secrets like passwords or API keys into an image is risky — anyone who pulls or inspects the image can read them back out of its layers, even ones from earlier build steps.
Secrets baked into an image can be ___ later.
Why avoid baking secrets into an image?
Secrets baked into an image live in its ___.
Deleting a secret later removes it from the image.
explanation: It can still be recovered from the earlier layer that added it.

prompt: By default a container's process runs as root inside the container, which is riskier if the app is ever compromised — switching to a non-root user limits what an attacker could do.
Which user should containers run as when possible?
Containers run as root by default unless told otherwise.
Running as a ___ user limits damage from hacks.
Why avoid running a container as root?
Starting FROM an untrusted or bloated base image can pull in vulnerabilities and unnecessary tools — prefer minimal, well-maintained, official base images instead.
A minimal, trusted base image is good ___ practice.
An untrusted base image can add ___.
What kind of base image is the safer choice?
Any image on Docker Hub is automatically safe.
explanation: Popularity isn't the same as trustworthiness — pick maintained, trusted sources.

prompt: Docker Hub is public by default, but a private registry keeps your images visible only to your own team or organization.
What does a private registry restrict?
explanation: Docker Hub itself is public by default — a private registry is the alternative when you don't want that.

prompt: Docker Hub images are public by default.
A ___ registry limits who can see an image.
Who might use a private registry?
docker push uploads a locally built image to a registry, and docker pull downloads it back down onto any other machine.
Complete: upload myapp to a registry.
docker push uploads an image to a registry.
docker ___ uploads a local image.
What does docker pull do?
docker system prune removes stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images all at once, freeing up disk space that piles up over time.
Complete: clean up unused resources.
explanation: Unused containers, networks, and images pile up over time until you clean them out.

prompt: Unused Docker resources can pile up over time.
docker system prune frees up disk ___.
What does prune remove?
Once you run containers across many machines, you need something to schedule, restart, and scale them automatically, which is exactly what an orchestrator like Kubernetes does.
When do you typically need an orchestrator?
explanation: It automatically schedules, restarts, and scales containers across those machines for you.

prompt: An orchestrator can restart failed containers automatically.
Kubernetes is an example of an ___.
What does an orchestrator automate?
Put a container's lifecycle stages in order.
Put these Dockerfile instructions in order.
explanation: Every Dockerfile starts FROM a base image, then COPY adds files, RUN installs or builds, and CMD sets what launches the container.

prompt: Put these multi-stage build steps in order.
options: Build stage compiles the app|Final stage copies only the built result

options: Build the image|Tag the image|Push the image to a registry
